title: Two boxed 128s
reveal:
false - and the same three lines with 127 instead print true.

`==` on two Integers compares references, never values. Autoboxing compiles to Integer.valueOf(int), which the language spec requires to return shared, cached objects for -128..127; past that it hands back a new object each time, so a and b are two objects and a == b is false.

Compare boxed values with equals(), or unbox one side so the comparison becomes numeric:

    a.equals(b)          // true
    a.intValue() == b    // true - one int operand unboxes the other

The cached range is a floor, not a ceiling: -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax can raise the upper bound (the lower one is fixed), so code that leans on == passing at 128 breaks on the next JVM. Boolean caches both values, Byte its whole range, Short/Integer/Long -128..127, Character 0..127 - and Double/Float cache nothing at all, so `Double x = 1.0, y = 1.0;` gives x == y false for every value there is.
